thought.text: The `--trust-lockfile` flag exists and is exactly for the "committed trusted lockfile" case. Let me start a resilient pnpm install in the background (skipping the flaky verification, lowering network concurrency to avoid ECONNRESET).

reasoning_content:
The flag exists. Next, let's start a resilient pnpm install in the background with a long timeout. This will probably take quite a while (huge frontend dependency tree, slow metadata). Let's use --trust-lockfile to skip the flaky verification (the lockfile is committed and trusted), and reduce network concurrency to avoid ECONNRESET.

Actually, wait — with --trust-lockfile the verification step gets skipped entirely, so it won't fetch all the metadata for the verification. That said, pnpm still needs to fetch metadata for dependency resolution, but... with a committed lockfile, pnpm installs directly from the lockfile (frozen-ish), so it downloads tarballs and links them. If there's a lockfile and no resolution is needed, metadata fetching is minimal (just tarball downloads).

Let's kick it off in the background, monitor it, and continue. This is going to take a while. Let's give it a long leash.

action.command:
cd /workspace/app && nohup pnpm install --trust-lockfile --network-concurrency 10 --fetch-concurrency 8 --fetch-timeout 120000 --fetch-retries 5 --fetch-retry-mintimeout 2000 --fetch-retry-maxtimeout 60000 > /tmp/pnpm-install.log 2>&1 &
echo "pnpm install pid $! started"; sleep 5; tail -5 /tmp/pnpm-install.log
